X-then-Y.reason: FIRST covers all ten brief items directly. Its ladder is an explicit, configurable list of model-and-effort rungs (haiku xhigh 2, sonnet high 1, sonnet xhigh 1, opus xhigh 1), so effort rises before model on both retry and escalate. The workflow passes an effort on every agent() call, ops included at low (item 7). aether-report lists each agent with its effort as well as byEffort per model (item 9). Old tier-only plans and old ladder lines still resolve to defaults. Its tests are exact and cover the tricky inputs: zero-attempt rungs, off-ladder starts, max, and relaunch against the plan's own ladder. The smoke run puts an implementer at medium against the file's xhigh, which proves the per-call override. Its weaknesses: one large coupled Task 1 (justified), a hardcoded machine path in the smoke run, an untested ad-hoc check script, and a supervisor fixed at xhigh rather than chosen per task. SECOND is well engineered: a tested check-effort script, a portable smoke run, a clear DAG and careful version/test coordination. But it deliberately omits effort on ops and reviewer calls, which contradicts item 7. Its report shows only role/model/effort aggregates, with no per-agent view (item 9 is partial). Its ladder stays per-model budgets with derived climbing, so escalation always jumps model, and a haiku-medium task climbs to haiku high then Sonnet, skipping the cheaper haiku xhigh. It also adds scope the brief did not ask for (Review line, climbed metric, version bump, tested tool), which pulls against the no-over-engineering preference. Its per-task Review line does match 'can be raised' more literally than FIRST's global xhigh supervisor.

Y-then-X.reason: FIRST is preferred, despite one gap against the brief. Its effort-first ladder is derived from the attempt count on each model, so it adds no new state and leaves the Ladder line unchanged. It keeps `tiers` and the escalation count meaning what they meant, and adds a separate `climbed` count. A per-task Review line makes the supervisor's effort raisable, which matches item 6 and stays cheap. Its contracts, exact tests and waves are tight: Tasks 1, 3, 4 and 5 run in parallel, then Task 2. Task 4 reads the version from the manifest so that Task 6's version bump keeps it green. The transcript checker, check-effort.js, is committed, has its own tests and is cross-checked against the report. The verification run is portable and shows that the per-call effort beats the agent file for both the implementer and the supervisor. FIRST's weaknesses: it deliberately passes no effort on ops and final-reviewer calls, which contradicts item 7 ('on each agent() call'). One refusal message also claims Sonnet at high beats Opus at medium, which the data does not support. Its docs task is a prose brief, not exact text. SECOND meets item 7 fully and models the ladder literally as model+effort rungs. But it adds a lot of machinery: a plan-written rung list with old, new and mixed forms, ordering validation, and off-ladder path building. It also changes `tiers` into step names, so an effort raise now counts as an escalation, which breaks comparability with past runs. It fixes the supervisor at xhigh for every task instead of making it raisable. It puts the parser, the compiler and the workflow into one large opus task. Its smoke run hardcodes a user-specific REPO path and relies on an untested ad-hoc script kept in a temp directory. SECOND's strong point is its docs task, which gives the exact text of every change.
